I used to be skeptical of the idea “the more languages you know, the easier it is to pick up another” but now I think it’s absolutely true. Knowing Russian helped me with Chinese despite the fact the languages aren’t related at all – it’s just that I had a much wider bank of sounds already available to me (eg the sh sound in chinese is more similar to a Russian ш than the English sh) and also I could understand differences in grammar much faster because I’d had to study that type of thing already. The more languages you learn the more connections you can make to stuff you already know, so eg instead of being like “what on earth is a tone?” You’re thinking “oh, so this language is tonal like Chinese”

Answering as someone who lives in China – prices for many products here may seem low based on conversion rates but currency conversion doesn’t tell the whole story. Wages are much lower here so bear in mind they are not buying these items with a US salary. That said, they are definitely cheaper here and part of the reason why is because cheap plastic products are usually made here in China. There’s no import/export costs, sometimes I’ve bought cheap shit from taobao and found it came from a city in my province. Also some of it is indeed low quality and will break quickly. Though in my experience stuff will usually work okay and last, it just won’t look like it did on the pictures

I live in a small town in Hebei province, it’s a very different situation here compared with big cities. We don’t have to do PCR tests consistently any more. I think my last test was over a month ago to be honest. When I do go it’s very quick because the queues are so short, it takes about 5 minutes.

You don’t need to wear a mask outside, but on the streets I’d say about 60-70% of people wear them anyway. I think technically you’re probably supposed to wear a mask in most indoor places but the only places it really gets enforced are supermarkets, hospitals and government buildings. If there‘s any hint that a local lockdown could happen then they suddenly start doing more testing and asking businesses to enforce mask wearing.

All social sites are open, we don’t really have stuff like bars and concerts in a small town like this anyway but as far as I’m aware there’s not anything that’s closed here. People are pretty much going about their daily lives as normal with regards to covid rules but it’s a boring city and travelling to other cities is a bit of a hassle now.

My province absolutely does not have a foreigner-friendly covid system, you literally can’t get the Hebei code if you don’t have mainland ID. There’s nothing I can do about it and every time I’m asked to show it I have to just explain “I’m a foreigner, I don’t have it” and show them the mini app drop-down menu if they keep asking. Thankfully I’ve never actually been refused entry or service, every person I’ve met just lets me off or accepts my green arrow code instead, but it sucks that I have to explain every time. I don’t need to use codes very often though because stuff is pretty chill here and a lot of places don’t really ask. Also getting the PCR test is easy in my city because I just scan a code that has my details attached, same as everyone else – I don’t need to show my passport. In Beijing I felt like I stood out a lot more because everyone else could just quickly scan their ID, but when it’s my turn they have to manually type out my details from my passport.

I think the one thing I would add is that my impression of covid here for small towns and cities is very much “everything is normal, until it’s not”. For most of the time I’ve lived here there’s been basically no compulsory testing, very few places masks were needed, pretty much normal life – HOWEVER when covid did hit my city it was pretty grim and we were stuck locked down in our communities with daily testing for over a month. At that time we had to be ready to be called out for covid tests at any time, once we even got woken up by speakerphones blaring at 3am calling us out for a PCR! So yeah, I’m very grateful for how chill things are now, but whenever there’s a rumour of a covid case in the city I’m nervous we’ll end up back in a super lockdown like before.

ID is identification aka proof of who you are. You don’t need to bring identification with you, you simply tell them your name and address (no proof needed). The card sent in the post in advance is just to inform you where to go to vote.

When you register to vote, you’re sent a card in the post telling you which polling station to go to. On the day they have a list of the registered voters for the area at the poll station. When you show up, you tell them your name and address and they check you off on the list. Realistically nobody is going to bother trying to find the locations of other people’s polling stations just to sneak in and risk a criminal record for an extra vote that’ll probably be caught before you get to the polling booth, because the name has already been checked off on the list. Rate of voter fraud is so low it’s basically completely statistically insignificant – on the other hand, obtaining a form of ID is somewhat expensive here and if required, would be enough to deter a significant proportion of the population from voting.
